source_refs.note: Exercise 6.5, Question 15 (book page 210); answer key PDF 308.

blocks.prompt: 15. Find the equations of the normals to the hyperbola \(\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1\) which are parallel to the line \(2x - y = 5\).
blocks.explanation:
A normal is the line through a point of the curve perpendicular to the tangent there.
"Parallel to \(2x - y = 5\)" fixes the slope of the normal: \(2\).
Plan: find the slope of the normal at \((x_1, y_1)\) as in Example 27, set it equal to 2, and look for a point of the hyperbola that satisfies this.
steps:
Given: \(\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1\), normals parallel to \(2x - y = 5\).
To find: the equations of such normals.
Method: Example 27 gives the slope of the tangent at \((x_1, y_1)\) as \(\frac{b^2 x_1}{a^2 y_1}\), so the normal has slope \(-\frac{a^2 y_1}{b^2 x_1}\). Equate it to 2 and solve together with the equation of the hyperbola.

Read \(a^2\), \(b^2\) and the required slope
\[a^2 = 9,\quad b^2 = 16\]
\[2x - y = 5 \Rightarrow y = 2x - 5\]
\[\text{Required slope} = 2\]
Why: Parallel lines have equal slopes.

Slope of the normal at \((x_1, y_1)\)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{b^2 x}{a^2 y} = \dfrac{16x}{9y}\]
\[m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{9y_1}{16x_1}\]
Why: Differentiating implicitly, as in Example 27. The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is the negative reciprocal.

Set the slope equal to 2
\[-\dfrac{9y_1}{16x_1} = 2\]
\[y_1 = -\dfrac{32x_1}{9}\]
Why: Cross-multiply: \(-9y_1 = 32x_1\).

The point must lie on the hyperbola
\[\dfrac{x_1^2}{9} - \dfrac{1}{16}\cdot\dfrac{1024x_1^2}{81} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{x_1^2}{9} - \dfrac{64x_1^2}{81} = 1\]
\[\dfrac{9x_1^2 - 64x_1^2}{81} = 1\]
\[x_1^2 = -\dfrac{81}{55}\]
Why: Substitute \(y_1 = -\frac{32x_1}{9}\), so \(y_1^2 = \frac{1024x_1^2}{81}\). A square of a real number cannot be negative, so there is no real point.

Why this happens
\[(x_1, y_1) = (3\sec\theta,\ 4\tan\theta)\]
\[m_{\text{normal}} = -\dfrac{9(4\tan\theta)}{16(3\sec\theta)}\]
\[= -\dfrac{3}{4}\sin\theta\]
Why: The book's parametric point. Since \(|\sin\theta| < 1\) on the hyperbola, every normal has slope between \(-\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{4}\). A slope of 2 is impossible.

Check
\[-\dfrac{3}{4}\sin\theta = 2\]
\[\sin\theta = -\dfrac{8}{3}\]
\[\left|-\dfrac{8}{3}\right| > 1\;\checkmark\]
Why: A slope of 2 would need \(\sin\theta = -\frac{8}{3}\), but no angle has a sine larger than 1 in size. Both methods (substitution and the parametric form) agree: no normal of this hyperbola has slope 2.
blocks.final_answer: No such normal exists: every normal to \(\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1\) has slope \(-\frac{3}{4}\sin\theta\), between \(-\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\frac{3}{4}\), so none is parallel to \(2x - y = 5\) (slope 2).

answer_figure.alt: The hyperbola x squared over 9 minus y squared over 16 equals 1 with vertices (3, 0) and (minus 3, 0) and dashed asymptotes y equals plus or minus four thirds x; the two answer-key lines y equals 2x plus or minus 14 over 5 pass between the branches without touching the curve.
answer_figure.caption: Answer figure: the answer key's lines y = 2x ± 14/5 never meet the hyperbola, so they cannot be normals (original drawing).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key prints \(5y = 10x - 14\) and \(5y = 10x + 14\), that is \(y = 2x \mp \frac{14}{5}\). These lines are not normals to \(\frac{x^2}{9} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1\); they do not even meet it. Putting \(y = 2x + k\) into \(16x^2 - 9y^2 = 144\) gives \(20x^2 + 36kx + 9k^2 + 144 = 0\), whose discriminant is \(576(k^2 - 20)\); for \(k^2 = \frac{196}{25} < 20\) it is negative. Correct answer: no normal to this hyperbola is parallel to \(2x - y = 5\).
